precepts.text: Under the goodly cedar shall dwell all fowl of every wing.
precepts.point: His boughs, Israel, were delivered to death in the nether parts of the earth, and the nations shook at his fall.

note.label: The Kingdom Of Adam And The Old World

precepts.why:
Ezekiel 31 says the great cedar was “of an high stature”, and “All the fowls of heaven made their nests in his boughs.” The fowls of heaven are the angels: all the angels were under Adam when he was ruling, as it says, “let all the angels of God worship him.” Under his branches the beasts of the field brought forth their young, and the serpent was “more subtil than any beast of the field”: Satan was there, under Adam. And “under his shadow dwelt all great nations”, all the nations of the earth.

Ezekiel 17 shows the same cedar planted again: “I will also take of the highest branch of the high cedar, and will set it; I will crop off from the top of his young twigs a tender one, and will plant it upon an high mountain and eminent.” That is talking about Christ. “In the mountain of the height of Israel will I plant it: and it shall bring forth boughs, and bear fruit, and be a goodly cedar: and under it shall dwell all fowl of every wing; in the shadow of the branches thereof shall they dwell.” That is the same as Ezekiel 31. He will plant it in the height of Israel, where it was before.

“And all the trees of the field shall know that I the Lord have brought down the high tree, have exalted the low tree, have dried up the green tree, and have made the dry tree to flourish.” He brought us down, and he raises us back up again. Ezra saw it too: on mount Sion, in the midst of a great people, “a young man of a high stature, taller than all the rest.”

To understand the kingdom of Adam you have to understand the kingdom that is to come. It will be the same thing: us ruling with Christ in righteousness, with all the fowl dwelling under the goodly cedar, and nobody able to hurt us.

precepts.text: The king commanded that certain children of Israel of the king's seed and princes, well favoured and skilful in wisdom, be taught the learning and tongue of the Chaldeans to stand in the king's palace.
precepts.point: When our people do well financially, get a good education, and buy into the pick-yourself-up-by-the-bootstraps idea that everyone has the same opportunity, the smart ones are removed from the ghetto so they will not be there to cause the uprising.

note.label: Ezekiel 17: The Riddle of the Two Eagles

precepts.why:
The king of Babylon “hath taken of the king’s seed” and “hath also taken the mighty of the land”. Daniel shows how it was done. The king told Ashpenaz, the master of his eunuchs, to bring “certain of the children of Israel, and of the king’s seed, and of the princes”: children “in whom was no blemish, but well favoured, and skilful in all wisdom, and cunning in knowledge, and understanding science”, such as had ability in them “to stand in the king’s palace”.

And what for? So that “they might teach the learning and the tongue of the Chaldeans.” The enemy takes the best and brightest and gives them the mind of the oppressor, so they are turned against their own people. That is how “the kingdom might be base, that it might not lift itself up”.

It is the same today. When our people do well financially, get a good education and buy into the pick-yourself-up-by-the-bootstraps idea that everyone has the same opportunity, the smart ones are removed from the ghetto. They will not be there to cause the uprising.

precepts.text: Nebuchadnezzar carried away all Jerusalem, the princes and mighty men of valour, craftsmen and smiths, leaving only the poorest sort, and made Mattaniah king, changing his name to Zedekiah.
precepts.point: When our people do well financially, get a good education, and buy into the pick-yourself-up-by-the-bootstraps idea that everyone has the same opportunity, the smart ones are removed from the ghetto so they will not be there to cause the uprising.

note.label: Ezekiel 17: The Riddle of the Two Eagles

precepts.why:
This is the history behind “the king of Babylon is come to Jerusalem, and hath taken the king thereof, and the princes thereof”. Nebuchadnezzar “carried away all Jerusalem, and all the princes, and all the mighty men of valour, even ten thousand captives, and all the craftsmen and smiths: none remained, save the poorest sort of the people of the land.”

He carried Jehoiachin to Babylon, with the king's mother, the king's wives, his officers and “the mighty of the land”: seven thousand men of might, a thousand craftsmen and smiths, “all that were strong and apt for war”. Then he “made Mattaniah his father’s brother king in his stead, and changed his name to Zedekiah.” That is the king's seed he made a covenant with and took an oath of.

The mighty, the skilled, the strong: everyone who could have lifted the kingdom up was taken, and only the poorest sort were left. That is what it means for the kingdom to be base, so that it might not lift itself up, but stand only by keeping his covenant.

precepts.text: The Greeks used the same strategy, taking our chief young men and teaching them heathenish Grecian ways, and they still do this today through sports academies.
precepts.point: When our people do well financially, get a good education, and buy into the pick-yourself-up-by-the-bootstraps idea that everyone has the same opportunity, the smart ones are removed from the ghetto so they will not be there to cause the uprising.

note.label: Ezekiel 17: The Riddle of the Two Eagles

precepts.why:
The Greeks used the same strategy as Babylon. Jason, “that ungodly wretch, and no high priest”, built “a place of exercise under the tower itself, and brought the chief young men under his subjection, and made them wear a hat.” The chief young men, the mighty of the land, brought under Greek subjection.

Such was “the height of Greek fashions, and increase of heathenish manners” that the priests “had no courage to serve any more at the altar”. They despised the temple, neglected the sacrifices and hastened to the place of exercise “after the game of Discus called them forth”, “Not setting by the honours of their fathers, but liking the glory of the Grecians best of all.”

Take the best and brightest, teach them heathenish Grecian ways, and they turn from their fathers to the glory of the oppressor. They still do this today through sports academies. It is the mighty of the land taken, so the kingdom stays base.

precepts.text: Not many wise, mighty, or noble are called, for the Most High has chosen the foolish and weak things of the world to confound the wise and mighty, so those on this reading are of no less value than anyone.
precepts.point: When our people do well financially, get a good education, and buy into the pick-yourself-up-by-the-bootstraps idea that everyone has the same opportunity, the smart ones are removed from the ghetto so they will not be there to cause the uprising.

note.label: Ezekiel 17: The Riddle of the Two Eagles

precepts.why:
The enemy takes the mighty, the best and the brightest. But look at who the Most High calls: “not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called”. Instead, “God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty”.

So the oppressor removing the smart ones from the ghetto does not stop the Most High. He works with those the world counts foolish and weak, and confounds the mighty with them.

Those on this reading are of no less value than anyone. The mighty of the land were carried away and taught the tongue of the Chaldeans; those the world counts foolish and weak are the ones He has chosen.

precepts.text: The scripture cannot be broken, so what the Most High has spoken concerning the low tree exalted and the high tree brought down He will surely do.
precepts.point: If the Most High has declared it, it shall come to pass, for the scripture cannot be broken.

note.label: Ezekiel 17: The Riddle of the Two Eagles

precepts.why:
Christ says “the scripture cannot be broken”. What the Most High has spoken, He will do; He says so Himself at the end of this passage: “I the Lord have spoken and have done it.”

So the whole thing is sure. He Himself takes of the highest branch of the high cedar, crops off a tender twig and plants it “upon an high mountain and eminent”, in the mountain of the height of Israel. It brings forth boughs, bears fruit and becomes a goodly cedar under which “all fowl of every wing” dwell. All the trees of the field know that He has “brought down the high tree”, “exalted the low tree”, dried up the green tree and made the dry tree flourish.

If the Most High has declared it, it shall come to pass. The low tree exalted and the high tree brought down is not a maybe, because the scripture cannot be broken.

points: The word of the Most High came to Ezekiel to put forth a riddle and speak a parable unto the house of Israel.

note.label: Ezekiel 17: The Riddle of the Two Eagles

points: A great eagle with great wings and divers colors came unto Lebanon, took the highest branch of the cedar, cropped off the top of his young twigs, and carried it into a land of traffic and a city of merchants.

note.label: Ezekiel 17: The Riddle of the Two Eagles

points: He took also of the seed of the land, planted it in a fruitful field by great waters, and it grew into a spreading vine of low stature whose branches turned toward him.

note.label: Ezekiel 17: The Riddle of the Two Eagles

points: There was another great eagle with great wings and many feathers, and this vine bent her roots and shot forth her branches toward him that he might water it, though it was already planted in good soil by great waters.

note.label: Ezekiel 17: The Riddle of the Two Eagles

points: The Most High asks whether it shall prosper; He shall pull up the roots and cut off the fruit that it wither, and when the east wind touches it, it shall utterly wither in the furrows where it grew.

note.label: Ezekiel 17: The Riddle of the Two Eagles

points: The Most High tells the rebellious house what these things mean: the king of Babylon came to Jerusalem, took the king and princes to Babylon, took of the king's seed, made a covenant and took an oath of him, and also took the mighty of the land.

note.label: Ezekiel 17: The Riddle of the Two Eagles

points: The enemy takes the mighty of the land, the best and brightest, and turns them against their people by giving them the mind of the oppressor, so the kingdom might be base and not lift itself up.

note.label: Ezekiel 17: The Riddle of the Two Eagles

points: The king rebelled against Babylon and sent ambassadors into Egypt for horses and much people; the Most High asks shall he prosper, shall he escape, or shall he break the covenant and be delivered.

note.label: Ezekiel 17: The Riddle of the Two Eagles

points: Because he despised the oath and broke the covenant after giving his hand, he shall die in the midst of Babylon, and Pharaoh with his mighty army shall not help him in the war.

note.label: Ezekiel 17: The Riddle of the Two Eagles

points: The Most High will spread His net upon him, take him in His snare, bring him to Babylon, and plead with him there; his fugitives shall fall by the sword and the remnant be scattered, and they shall know that He is the Lord.

note.label: Ezekiel 17: The Riddle of the Two Eagles

points: The Most High will Himself take of the highest branch of the high cedar, crop off a tender twig, and plant it upon the high mountain in the height of Israel.

note.label: Ezekiel 17: The Riddle of the Two Eagles
